q: The purchase by a non-financial enterprise of shares of another company, held as a long-term investment, is classified in its cash flow statement as a cash flow from:

options.A: Operating activities
options.B: Financing activities
options.C: No activity, because shares are not assets
options.D: Investing activities

e: Purchase of shares of another company as a long-term investment is acquisition of an investment asset, hence a cash flow from investing activities.

q: An amount transferred to the general reserve out of the profits of the year is dealt with in computing the funds from operations by:

options.A: Deducting it from the net profit, as it is an outflow of funds
options.B: Adding it back to the net profit, because it is only an appropriation of profit and involves no outflow of funds
options.C: Showing it as a separate source of funds
options.D: Ignoring it, because reserves do not appear in the profit and loss account

e: Transfer to general reserve is only an appropriation of profit with no outflow of funds, so it is added back to net profit in computing funds from operations.

q: The direct and the indirect methods of presenting cash flow from operating activities in a cash flow statement differ in that:

options.A: The two methods give different amounts of net cash from operating activities
options.B: The direct method is used only by financial enterprises
options.C: They differ only in the manner of presenting the operating activities, the net cash from operating activities being the same under both, while investing and financing activities are presented identically
options.D: The indirect method does not require the balance sheet of the enterprise

e: Direct and indirect methods differ only in presentation of operating activities; both give the same net cash from operating activities, and investing and financing sections are identical under both.

q: A bank overdraft which is repayable on demand and forms an integral part of an enterprise's cash management is, for the purpose of the cash flow statement, treated as:

options.A: A component of cash and cash equivalents
options.B: A long-term borrowing under financing activities in every case
options.C: An item of the profit and loss account
options.D: A part of the inventories of the enterprise

e: A bank overdraft repayable on demand that forms an integral part of cash management is treated as a component of cash and cash equivalents for cash flow statement purposes.

q: An enterprise issues bonus shares to its existing shareholders by capitalising a part of its general reserve. In the fund flow statement, this transaction results in:

options.A: A source of funds equal to the value of the bonus shares
options.B: An application of funds equal to the value of the bonus shares
options.C: An increase in the working capital of the enterprise
options.D: No flow of funds, because it involves only two non-current items, share capital and reserves, and causes no change in working capital

e: Bonus shares issued by capitalising general reserve involve only two non-current items, share capital and reserves, with no change in working capital, so there is no flow of funds.

q: The sales mix variance, computed on the margin (profit) basis, arises when:

options.A: The proportion in which the different products are actually sold differs from the proportion in which they were budgeted to be sold
options.B: The actual selling price of a product differs from its budgeted selling price
options.C: The total quantity of products actually sold differs from the total budgeted quantity, the mix remaining unchanged
options.D: The fixed costs of the period exceed the budgeted fixed costs

e: Sales mix variance on the margin basis arises when the proportion in which different products are actually sold differs from the budgeted proportion.

q: The budgeted fixed overheads of a factory for a period are Rs 3,00,000, while the actual fixed overheads incurred are Rs 3,27,000. The fixed overhead expenditure variance is:

options.A: Rs 27,000 (Favourable)
options.B: Rs 3,000 (Adverse)
options.C: Rs 27,000 (Adverse)
options.D: Nil

e: Fixed overhead expenditure variance = actual fixed overheads - budgeted fixed overheads = 327000 - 300000 = Rs 27000 Adverse.

q: The labour gang (composition) variance arises when:

options.A: The actual wage rate paid differs from the standard wage rate
options.B: Workers remain idle due to a power failure during the period
options.C: The actual hours worked exceed the standard hours for the output
options.D: The actual composition of the labour gang — the proportions of skilled, semi-skilled and unskilled workers — differs from the standard composition of the gang

e: Labour gang or composition variance arises when the actual composition of the gang, the proportions of skilled, semi-skilled and unskilled workers, differs from the standard composition.

q: Budgeted production overheads are Rs 2,50,000 for 25,000 budgeted hours, giving a standard fixed overhead rate of Rs 10 per hour. The hours actually made available (capacity hours) during the period are 22,000. The fixed overhead capacity variance is:

options.A: Rs 30,000 (Adverse)
options.B: Rs 30,000 (Favourable)
options.C: Rs 25,000 (Adverse)
options.D: Rs 22,000 (Adverse)

e: Fixed overhead capacity variance = (capacity hours - budgeted hours) x standard rate = (22000 - 25000) x 10 = Rs 30000 Adverse.

q: In the simultaneous equation method of secondary distribution of overheads:

options.A: The cost of each service department is distributed only once, in a fixed sequence, and is never revisited
options.B: The interdependence of service departments is fully recognised by setting up equations for the total cost of each service department, including the share it receives from other service departments, and solving them together
options.C: Services rendered by one service department to another are ignored altogether
options.D: Overheads are absorbed directly into products without any distribution to production departments

e: The simultaneous equation method fully recognises interdependence of service departments by setting up equations for each service department total cost including shares received from others, and solving them together.

q: A factory's budgeted fixed overheads are Rs 2,40,000 for a month budgeted to have 24 working days. The month actually had 26 working days. The fixed overhead calendar variance is:

options.A: Rs 10,000 (Favourable)
options.B: Rs 20,000 (Adverse)
options.C: Rs 20,000 (Favourable)
options.D: Rs 24,000 (Favourable)

e: Budgeted cost per day = 240000 / 24 = Rs 10000. Calendar variance = (26 - 24) x 10000 = Rs 20000 Favourable, because two extra working days were available.

q: Under the direct distribution method of secondary distribution:

options.A: Service department costs are apportioned only to production departments, ignoring the services that service departments render to one another
options.B: Service departments are closed one by one in a prescribed order
options.C: Algebraic equations are solved to find the true cost of each service department
options.D: Service department costs are written off to the Costing Profit and Loss Account

e: Under the direct distribution method, service department costs are apportioned only to production departments, ignoring services that service departments render to one another.

q: The standard selling price of a product is Rs 80 per unit. The actual selling price realised is Rs 76 per unit and the actual quantity sold is 6,000 units. The sales price variance is:

options.A: Rs 4,000 (Adverse)
options.B: Rs 24,000 (Favourable)
options.C: Rs 24,000 (Adverse)
options.D: Rs 48,000 (Adverse)

e: Sales price variance = (actual price - standard price) x actual quantity = (76 - 80) x 6000 = Rs 24000 Adverse.

q: For the actual output, the standard quantity of a material is 5,000 kg. Because the total material input actually used differs from the standard input, the revised standard quantity (the standard quantity re-worked in the standard proportion for the actual total input) is 5,400 kg. The standard price is Rs 15 per kg. The material revised usage variance is:

options.A: Rs 6,000 (Adverse)
options.B: Rs 6,000 (Favourable)
options.C: Rs 81,000 (Favourable)
options.D: Rs 75,000 (Adverse)

e: Material revised usage variance = (standard quantity - revised standard quantity) x standard price = (5000 - 5400) x 15 = Rs 6000 Adverse.

q: After primary distribution, the total cost of the Stores service department is Rs 90,000. It is apportioned on an agreed basis: 50% to Production Department A, 30% to Production Department B and 20% to the Canteen service department, whose cost is distributed next under the step method. The amount apportioned to Production Department A at this step is:
e: Amount apportioned to Production Department A = 50 percent of 90000 = Rs 45000 under the agreed basis at this step of the step method.

q: 'Multiple costing' (composite costing) is the method applied where:

options.A: A product is assembled from a number of separate components, each produced by a different method of manufacture, so that the total cost of the finished product is built up by combining the costs ascertained under different costing methods for its parts
options.B: A single homogeneous product is produced continuously in bulk quantities
options.C: Each customer's order is costed separately from start to finish as one job
options.D: A service is rendered to customers and the cost per unit of service is ascertained

e: Multiple or composite costing applies where a product is assembled from separate components each produced by a different method, so total cost combines costs ascertained under different costing methods for its parts.

q: Standing charges relating to a machine for a month are: share of rent Rs 7,000, insurance Rs 3,000, share of supervision Rs 4,000 and lighting Rs 2,000. Effective working hours are 200 per month. Running charges per hour are: depreciation Rs 60 (machine cost Rs 7,20,000, effective life 12,000 hours), power Rs 45, repairs Rs 25 and consumable stores Rs 10. The comprehensive machine hour rate is:

options.A: Rs 140 per hour
options.B: Rs 180 per hour
options.C: Rs 220 per hour
options.D: Rs 300 per hour

e: Standing charges = 7000 + 3000 + 4000 + 2000 = Rs 16000, per hour = 16000 / 200 = Rs 80. Running charges per hour = depreciation 60 + power 45 + repairs 25 + stores 10 = Rs 140. Machine hour rate = 80 + 140 = Rs 220 per hour.

q: Where a by-product is recovered in a process and has a realisable value, a commonly followed treatment in arriving at the cost of the main product is to:

options.A: Add the realisable value of the by-product to the joint cost of the process
options.B: Ignore the by-product completely in the cost accounts
options.C: Charge the entire joint cost to the by-product alone
options.D: Deduct the net realisable value of the by-product from the total process (joint) cost, so that the main product bears only the balance cost

e: The net realisable value of a by-product is deducted from the total process or joint cost, so the main product bears only the balance cost.

q: Budgeted hours of a department are 12,000. Actual hours worked are 9,600 and the standard hours for the actual output achieved are 10,800. The efficiency ratio is:
e: Efficiency ratio = standard hours for actual output / actual hours x 100 = 10800 / 9600 x 100 = 112.5 percent.

q: In a break-even chart, the margin of safety at a given level of sales is represented by:

options.A: The distance between the break-even point and the point representing the actual (or budgeted) level of sales
options.B: The vertical distance between the sales line and the fixed cost line at the origin
options.C: The angle between the total cost line and the sales line
options.D: The height of the fixed cost line above the horizontal axis

e: In a break-even chart the margin of safety is the distance between the break-even point and the point representing the actual or budgeted level of sales.

q: From the following data, the works cost of a product is: direct material consumed Rs 3,20,000; direct labour Rs 1,80,000; direct (chargeable) expenses Rs 50,000; factory overheads Rs 1,10,000:
e: Works cost = 320000 + 180000 + 50000 + 110000 = Rs 660000, being prime cost plus factory overheads.

q: In a process, 12,000 units were completed and transferred to the next process during a period. Closing work-in-progress is 3,000 units, which are complete as to material but only 40% complete as to conversion (labour and overhead) cost. The equivalent production in respect of conversion cost is:

options.A: 15,000 units
options.B: 13,200 units
options.C: 12,000 units
options.D: 10,800 units

e: Equivalent production for conversion = completed units 12000 + closing work-in-progress 3000 x 40 percent = 12000 + 1200 = 13200 units.

q: Under inter-process profit accounting, where the output of one process is transferred to the next process at cost plus a mark-up, the profit element included in the closing stock of the receiving process is:

options.A: Treated as realised profit of the period in full
options.B: Ignored, because all inter-process transfers are internal
options.C: Added to the cost of the closing stock for balance sheet purposes
options.D: Unrealised profit, for which a stock reserve is created so that the closing stock is shown at its actual cost to the factory as a whole

e: Profit included in closing stock transferred at cost plus mark-up is unrealised for the factory as a whole, so a stock reserve is created and the stock is shown at actual cost.

q: In a process, 4,000 units are introduced at a total cost of Rs 1,84,000. Normal loss is 10% of input and the scrap realises Rs 10 per unit. Actual output is 3,400 units. The value of the abnormal loss is:
e: Cost per good unit = (184000 - normal loss scrap 400 x 10) / 3600 = 180000 / 3600 = Rs 50. Abnormal loss = 3600 - 3400 = 200 units, value = 200 x 50 = Rs 10000.

q: Retention money in a contract account refers to:

options.A: The portion of the value of work certified that is withheld by the contractee and paid only after satisfactory completion, as a security for due performance
options.B: The penalty deducted from the contractor for delayed completion of the work
options.C: The profit retained in the contract account as a reserve
options.D: The amount of cash the contractor keeps in hand at the site

e: Retention money is the portion of the value of work certified withheld by the contractee as security for due performance, paid only after satisfactory completion.

q: A joint cost of Rs 4,80,000 is to be apportioned between Products A and B by the net realisable value method. A: final sales value Rs 6,00,000, further processing cost Rs 1,50,000. B: final sales value Rs 4,00,000, further processing cost Rs 1,00,000. The share of joint cost borne by Product A is:
Work uncertified at the end of an accounting period in a contract is valued for the contract account at:

options.A: Its market value
options.B: Cost plus a proportionate share of the notional profit
options.C: Its cost, without adding any element of profit
options.D: The value at which the architect is expected to certify it in the next period

e: Work uncertified is valued at cost only, without adding any element of profit, because it has not yet been certified by the architect.

q: A manufacturer produces a component in batches of 400 units. Set-up cost is Rs 2,000 per batch. Material cost is Rs 55 per unit and labour cost is Rs 35 per unit. Ignoring other overheads, the batch cost per unit is:

options.A: Rs 90
options.B: Rs 95
options.C: Rs 92
options.D: Rs 85

e: Set-up cost per unit = 2000 / 400 = Rs 5. Batch cost per unit = 55 + 35 + 5 = Rs 95.

q: In contract costing, where the work certified exceeds one-half of the contract price, the profit to be credited to the Profit and Loss Account is commonly taken as:

options.A: Two-thirds of the notional profit, reduced in the proportion that cash received bears to the work certified
options.B: The whole of the notional profit, irrespective of cash received
options.C: One-third of the notional profit, without any adjustment for cash received
options.D: The cash received minus the cost of work certified

e: Where work certified exceeds one-half of the contract price, profit credited is commonly two-thirds of notional profit, reduced in the proportion that cash received bears to work certified.

q: The value of work certified under a contract is Rs 12,00,000 and the cost of the work certified is Rs 9,00,000. Cash received is 75% of the work certified, and the work certified exceeds one-half of the contract price. Using the rule of two-thirds of notional profit adjusted for cash received, the profit to be credited to the Profit and Loss Account is:
e: Notional profit = 1200000 - 900000 = Rs 300000. Profit credited = 2/3 x 300000 x 75 percent = Rs 150000.

q: Actual sales of a firm are Rs 40,00,000 and its break-even sales are Rs 26,00,000. The margin of safety ratio (margin of safety as a percentage of actual sales) is:
e: Margin of safety = actual sales - break-even sales = 4000000 - 2600000 = Rs 1400000. Ratio = 1400000 / 4000000 x 100 = 35 percent.

q: A predetermined overhead absorption rate is preferred to an actual rate computed after the period ends mainly because:

options.A: It guarantees that there will never be any under-absorption or over-absorption of overheads
options.B: It is prescribed by the Companies Act for all factories
options.C: It enables product costs to be ascertained promptly during the period and avoids month-to-month fluctuations in unit cost caused by seasonal variations in overheads or output
options.D: It eliminates the need for any primary distribution of overheads

e: A predetermined absorption rate allows product costs to be ascertained promptly during the period and avoids month-to-month fluctuations in unit cost from seasonal variations in overheads or output.

q: A product sells for Rs 400 per unit. Its variable cost per unit is: direct material Rs 130, direct labour Rs 80 and variable overheads Rs 50. The P/V ratio of the product is:
e: Variable cost = 130 + 80 + 50 = Rs 260. Contribution = 400 - 260 = Rs 140. P/V ratio = 140 / 400 x 100 = 35 percent.

q: Under the cost-plus-on-marginal-cost method of pricing a special job, the price is fixed by:

options.A: Taking the marginal (variable) cost of the job and adding an agreed percentage contribution towards fixed costs and profit
options.B: Adding the desired profit to the total cost including all allocated fixed overheads
options.C: Copying the price charged by the nearest competitor
options.D: Dividing the total fixed cost by the expected number of units

e: Under cost-plus on marginal cost, price is the marginal or variable cost of the job plus an agreed percentage contribution towards fixed costs and profit.

q: A firm's fixed costs are revised upward to Rs 4,80,000 for the coming year. The contribution is Rs 60 per unit and the firm wishes to earn a target profit of Rs 1,80,000. The number of units it must sell is:

options.A: 8,000 units
options.B: 3,000 units
options.C: 11,000 units
options.D: 5,000 units

e: Units required = (fixed costs + target profit) / contribution per unit = (480000 + 180000) / 60 = 660000 / 60 = 11000 units.

q: In strategic cost management, 'executional cost drivers' are factors that:

options.A: Determine the firm's cost position through its basic structural choices of scale and scope
options.B: Reflect how efficiently a firm carries out its activities — such as workforce commitment and involvement, total quality management, capacity utilisation and the efficiency of plant layout
options.C: Are imposed on the firm by government regulation alone
options.D: Remain unchanged whatever management does in the short or long run

e: Executional cost drivers reflect how efficiently a firm carries out its activities, such as workforce commitment, total quality management, capacity utilisation and plant layout efficiency.

q: A division has capital employed of Rs 15,00,000 and earns a profit of Rs 2,70,000. The cost of capital is 12%. The Residual Income of the division is:
e: Residual Income = profit - cost of capital charge = 270000 - 12 percent x 1500000 = 270000 - 180000 = Rs 90000.

q: A known limitation of judging a division by Return on Investment (ROI) alone is that:

options.A: ROI can never be computed for a division that also sells to outside customers
options.B: A divisional manager may reject a project that is profitable for the company as a whole because accepting it would reduce the division's own ROI
options.C: ROI takes into account the cost of capital of the enterprise
options.D: ROI always encourages managers to over-invest in new assets

e: Judging solely by ROI can make a divisional manager reject a project profitable for the company as a whole because accepting it would reduce the divisions own ROI.

q: The standard fixed overhead rate is Rs 12 per hour. The standard hours for the actual output are 6,000, while the actual hours worked are 6,500. The fixed overhead efficiency variance is:

options.A: Rs 6,000 (Favourable)
options.B: Rs 78,000 (Adverse)
options.C: Rs 72,000 (Favourable)
options.D: Rs 6,000 (Adverse)

e: Fixed overhead efficiency variance = (standard hours - actual hours) x standard rate = (6000 - 6500) x 12 = Rs 6000 Adverse.

q: In the Theory of Constraints, an hour saved at a non-bottleneck resource:

options.A: Increases the throughput of the whole factory by the same amount
options.B: Is largely a mirage — it does not increase the throughput of the system, because the system's output is governed by the bottleneck resource
options.C: Reduces the work-in-progress of the bottleneck resource automatically
options.D: Must always be used to produce more work-in-progress for stock

e: System output is governed by the bottleneck resource, so an hour saved at a non-bottleneck resource is largely a mirage and does not increase throughput of the whole factory.

q: A product gives a throughput of Rs 450 per unit and takes 0.75 hour on the bottleneck machine. The operating (factory) cost is Rs 480 per bottleneck hour. The Throughput Accounting Ratio is:
e: Throughput per bottleneck hour = 450 / 0.75 = Rs 600. Throughput Accounting Ratio = 600 / 480 = 1.25.

q: Which of the following is an appraisal (detection) cost under the classification of quality costs?

options.A: Cost of inspecting and testing incoming materials and finished products before despatch
options.B: Cost of reworking defective units detected within the factory
options.C: Cost of warranty claims made by customers after sale
options.D: Cost of training workers in quality methods

e: Inspecting and testing incoming materials and finished products before despatch is an appraisal or detection cost, incurred to detect defects before the product reaches the customer.

q: The cost of scrap arising in production, rework of defective units and downtime caused by poor quality, all detected before the product reaches the customer, are classified as:

options.A: Prevention costs
options.B: Appraisal costs
options.C: External failure costs
options.D: Internal failure costs

e: Scrap, rework of defective units and downtime from poor quality detected before the product reaches the customer are internal failure costs.

q: Total Quality Management (TQM) approaches the cost of quality primarily by emphasising:

options.A: More and more inspection at the end of the production line
options.B: Prevention and building quality into the process — doing things right the first time — so that failure and appraisal costs fall over time
options.C: Accepting a fixed percentage of defective output as unavoidable
options.D: Charging all quality costs to the customer through higher prices

e: TQM emphasises prevention and building quality into the process, doing things right the first time, so that failure and appraisal costs fall over time.

q: Competitive benchmarking, as a cost and performance improvement technique, involves:

options.A: Comparing a firm's processes and performance only with its own past results
options.B: Comparing the budgets of two departments of the same firm with each other
options.C: Fixing the firm's prices exactly equal to the lowest price in the market
options.D: Comparing the firm's products, processes and costs with those of the best-performing competitors or recognised leaders, and adopting the practices that explain their superior performance

e: Competitive benchmarking compares the firms products, processes and costs with those of best-performing competitors or recognised leaders and adopts the practices explaining their superior performance.

q: Business Process Re-engineering (BPR) is best described as:

options.A: Making small, gradual improvements to an existing process
options.B: Transferring a process to an outside contractor at a lower price
options.C: Preparing a fresh budget for a process from the zero base
options.D: The fundamental rethinking and radical redesign of business processes to achieve dramatic improvements in cost, quality and speed

e: Business Process Re-engineering is the fundamental rethinking and radical redesign of business processes to achieve dramatic improvements in cost, quality and speed.

q: In Porter's value chain analysis, which of the following is a primary activity?

options.A: Human resource management
options.B: Procurement of materials
options.C: Inbound logistics — receiving, storing and distributing inputs for production
options.D: Firm infrastructure and general administration

e: Inbound logistics, receiving, storing and distributing inputs for production, is a primary activity in Porters value chain; human resource management, procurement and firm infrastructure are support activities.

q: Structural cost drivers in strategic cost management are factors that:

options.A: Arise from day-to-day operating decisions such as the degree of capacity utilisation
options.B: Determine a firm's underlying cost structure through fundamental choices about scale, scope, experience, technology and product complexity
options.C: Are fixed by the government for all firms in an industry
options.D: Can be changed freely in the very short run without any commitment

e: Structural cost drivers determine a firms underlying cost structure through fundamental choices about scale, scope, experience, technology and product complexity.

q: Life-cycle costing of a product, in its full sense, takes into account:

options.A: Only the manufacturing cost incurred up to the point of sale
options.B: Only the research and development cost incurred before production begins
options.C: Costs of all stages of the product's life — design and development, production, marketing and distribution, and also downstream costs borne after sale such as maintenance support, warranty service and eventual disposal
options.D: Only the costs that vary with the number of units produced

e: Life-cycle costing covers all stages of a products life: design and development, production, marketing and distribution, and downstream costs after sale such as maintenance, warranty service and disposal.

q: In target costing, value engineering is used mainly to:

options.A: Raise the allowable cost of the product after production has begun
options.B: Transfer product design work entirely to the suppliers of materials
options.C: Increase the number of components in the product to raise its selling price
options.D: Examine the functions of the product and its components systematically so that the product delivers the required functions and quality at a cost not exceeding the target cost

e: Value engineering systematically examines the functions of the product and its components so the product delivers required functions and quality at a cost not exceeding the target cost.

q: A machine can be bought outright or taken on lease for 3 years at a rental of Rs 1,20,000 payable at the end of each year. At a discount rate of 10% (annuity factor for 3 years = 2.487), the present value of the lease rentals, which is compared with the cost of buying in a lease-versus-buy appraisal, is:
e: Present value of lease rentals = Rs 1,20,000 x 2.487 = Rs 2,98,440. In a lease-versus-buy appraisal this discounted value of the rental stream, not the undiscounted total of Rs 3,60,000, is compared with the purchase cost.

q: The specific cost of capital of a project, as distinct from the composite (weighted average) cost of capital of the enterprise, is the cost that is relevant when:

options.A: The funds for the project are raised from one identified source and the discount rate is matched to that source and the project's own risk
options.B: The project is financed entirely from retained earnings
options.C: The project is a replacement proposal
options.D: The enterprise has no debt in its capital structure

e: Specific cost of capital is the cost of the particular source actually used for a project. It is relevant when funds come from one identified source, so the discount rate is matched to that source and to the project's own risk, unlike the composite weighted average cost.

q: In the appraisal of public-sector projects, the 'hurdle rate' means:

options.A: The highest rate of interest charged by any lender to the project
options.B: The rate of inflation expected over the project life
options.C: The minimum rate of return a project must promise before it can be accepted
options.D: The average rate of return earned on past projects

e: A hurdle rate is the minimum acceptable rate of return in project appraisal. A project is accepted only if its expected return meets or exceeds this cut-off; a lower return leads to rejection even if it is positive.

q: In social cost-benefit analysis, 'shadow pricing' of an input or output means valuing it at:

options.A: Its controlled (administered) market price
options.B: A notional price reflecting its true economic opportunity cost to society, where the market price is distorted
options.C: Its price in the previous year, adjusted for profit margin
options.D: The price charged by the cheapest supplier

e: Shadow pricing values an input or output at a notional price reflecting its true economic opportunity cost to society. It is used in social cost-benefit analysis where market prices are distorted by taxes, controls or monopoly and do not show real economic worth.

q: The Little-Mirrlees approach to social cost-benefit analysis, as distinct from the UNIDO approach, is characterised by valuing project inputs and outputs at:

options.A: Domestic market prices, with aggregate consumption as the numeraire
options.B: Shadow prices fixed by the Planning Commission for each industry
options.C: Historical cost, with tax collections as the numeraire
options.D: World (border) prices, with uncommitted social income measured in foreign exchange as the numeraire

e: The Little-Mirrlees approach values project inputs and outputs at world or border prices. Its numeraire is uncommitted social income measured in foreign exchange, whereas the UNIDO approach uses domestic prices with aggregate consumption as the numeraire.

q: Where two mutually exclusive assets have unequal lives and the service is needed indefinitely, the 'replacement chain' (common life) method of comparison works by:

options.A: Ignoring the asset with the shorter life altogether
options.B: Repeating each asset over a common time horizon (the least common multiple of lives) and comparing the net present values over that horizon
options.C: Comparing only the first cycle of each asset, without repetition
options.D: Comparing the assets on their accounting rates of return over their own lives

e: The replacement chain method repeats each asset over a common horizon equal to the least common multiple of the two lives. The net present values over that repeated common period are then comparable, since both provide service for the same length of time.

q: A project requires an outlay of Rs 6,00,000. Its cash inflows, already stated in nominal (money) terms, are Rs 3,00,000 at the end of Year 1 and Rs 4,00,000 at the end of Year 2, and are discounted at the nominal rate of 10% (factors: Year 1 = 0.909, Year 2 = 0.826). The Net Present Value is:
e: Present value of inflows = Rs 3,00,000 x 0.909 + Rs 4,00,000 x 0.826 = Rs 2,72,700 + Rs 3,30,400 = Rs 6,03,100. NPV = Rs 6,03,100 - Rs 6,00,000 = Rs 3,100, using nominal cash flows with the nominal discount rate.

q: A project's Year 1 cash inflow is estimated at Rs 2,00,000 at today's prices. With expected inflation of 5%, the nominal (money) cash inflow to be shown for Year 1, for discounting at the nominal discount rate, is:
e: Nominal cash flow = real cash flow inflated for expected inflation, that is Rs 2,00,000 x 1.05 = Rs 2,10,000. Nominal flows must be paired with a nominal discount rate, just as real flows are paired with a real rate.

q: A 'real option' in project appraisal, which a conventional static net present value calculation tends to ignore, is:

options.A: The value of managerial flexibility, such as the options to defer, expand or abandon a project as conditions unfold
options.B: The option of the lender to recall the loan before maturity
options.C: The option of shareholders to sell their shares in the market
options.D: The option of converting debentures into equity shares

e: A real option is the value of managerial flexibility built into a project, such as the options to defer, expand or abandon it as conditions unfold. A static NPV assumes a fixed course of action and therefore tends to ignore this flexibility value.

q: The abandonment value of a project becomes decisive in appraisal when:

options.A: It is lower than the book value of the project's assets
options.B: It exceeds the present value of the cash flows from continuing the project, so that abandoning yields more than continuing
options.C: The project has not yet reached its payback point
options.D: The project's salvage value at the end of its full life is nil

e: Abandonment is worthwhile when the abandonment value exceeds the present value of the cash flows from continuing the project. Continuing then destroys value, because the assets are worth more realised now than kept in operation.

q: Two projects have identical cash flows in every year, but the book (accounting) rate of return shows them differently only because different methods of depreciation are charged on them. This illustrates that the book rate of return is criticised because it:

options.A: Uses cash flows instead of accounting profits
options.B: Is too difficult for non-accountants to understand
options.C: Depends on accounting conventions such as the depreciation method, rather than on the underlying cash flows
options.D: Considers the time value of money in full

e: The book or accounting rate of return is based on accounting profit, which changes with conventions such as the depreciation method even when cash flows are identical. It therefore measures accounting treatment rather than the project's underlying cash economics, and it also ignores time value.

q: The 'bail-out payback period' of a project differs from the ordinary payback period in that, in judging recovery of the outlay, it also takes into account:

options.A: The interest payable on the funds invested
options.B: The tax saving on depreciation
options.C: The estimated resale (salvage) value of the asset at each point of time, along with the cash inflows received up to that point
options.D: The cash inflows expected after the payback point

e: The bail-out payback period checks, at each point, whether cash inflows received so far plus the estimated resale or salvage value of the asset at that point cover the original outlay. Recovery is thus judged with an exit value included, unlike ordinary payback.

q: Ranking projects by Profitability Index maximises the total net present value of the accepted set reliably only when the projects are divisible. Where projects are indivisible (lumpy), the correct approach under a funds constraint is to:

options.A: Accept projects strictly in Profitability Index order, even if funds are left idle
options.B: Reject all projects with a Profitability Index below 2
options.C: Rank projects by payback period instead
options.D: Examine feasible combinations of projects within the funds available and choose the combination giving the highest total net present value

e: With indivisible projects, following Profitability Index order can leave funds idle and miss the best set. The correct approach is to examine all feasible combinations within the funds available and select the combination with the highest total NPV.

q: In government and railway capital budgeting, financial justification and sanction of a work do not by themselves authorise expenditure because, in addition, the expenditure requires:

options.A: A separate sanction from the Comptroller and Auditor General
options.B: A viability gap funding grant from the Central Government
options.C: Approval of the work by the Zonal Railway Users' Consultative Committee
options.D: Provision of funds in the budget (appropriation) for the year in which the expenditure is to be incurred

e: Sanction and financial justification of a work do not themselves authorise spending. Expenditure can be incurred only when funds are provided in the budget or appropriation for the year of spending, which is a separate and necessary authority.

q: A work is expected to yield a net saving of Rs 60,000 in the first year, growing at 2% per year indefinitely thereafter. At a discount rate of 12%, the present value of this growing perpetuity, computed as first-year saving divided by (discount rate minus growth rate), is:
e: Present value of a growing perpetuity = Rs 60,000 / (0.12 - 0.02) = Rs 60,000 / 0.10 = Rs 6,00,000. The formula divides the first-year amount by the discount rate minus the constant growth rate.

q: In computing the cash flows of a project for financial appraisal, interest on the capital invested in the project is not deducted as a cash outflow mainly because:

options.A: Interest is never an expense of the enterprise
options.B: The cost of funds is already reflected in the rate at which the cash flows are discounted, so deducting interest as well would count it twice
options.C: Interest is always paid out of the current year's revenue budget
options.D: Interest payments are exempt from tax

e: Interest on project capital is not deducted from project cash flows because the cost of funds is already captured in the discount rate. Deducting interest as an outflow as well would count the financing cost twice in the appraisal.

q: 'Hard' capital rationing, as distinct from 'soft' capital rationing, arises when:

options.A: Management itself fixes a ceiling on capital expenditure as a matter of internal policy
options.B: A department chooses to postpone a project to the next plan period
options.C: The sanctioning authority asks for a revised estimate of the project
options.D: The enterprise is unable to raise funds from the capital market at any acceptable terms, so the constraint is imposed from outside

e: Hard capital rationing is imposed from outside, when the enterprise cannot raise funds in the capital market on acceptable terms. Soft rationing, by contrast, is a self-imposed internal ceiling fixed by management as a matter of policy.

q: For purposes of financial appraisal, the life over which a project's cash flows are projected should be its:

options.A: Economic life, that is, the period over which it remains worthwhile to operate it, which may be shorter than its physical or technical life
options.B: Physical life, however long the asset may last physically
options.C: Life as fixed in the depreciation schedule for tax purposes only
options.D: Life of the longest-lived asset already owned by the enterprise

e: Project cash flows should be projected over the economic life, the period over which operating the project remains worthwhile. This may be shorter than the physical or technical life, and cash flows beyond the economic life have no appraisal value.

q: Where the net present value and internal rate of return of two mutually exclusive projects of different size conflict, examining the internal rate of return on the incremental (difference) cash flows of the larger project over the smaller helps because it shows whether:

options.A: The smaller project should be abandoned altogether
options.B: The payback period of the larger project is shorter
options.C: The extra outlay on the larger project earns at least the required rate of return
options.D: The two projects can be combined into one project

e: Incremental IRR tests the extra outlay of the larger project against its extra cash flows over the smaller project. If the incremental return is at least the required rate, the additional investment is justified and the larger project is preferred.

q: Scenario analysis of a project, as distinct from sensitivity analysis, examines the effect on the project's result of:

options.A: A consistent set of several variables changing together, as in an optimistic or a pessimistic scenario
options.B: Changing one key variable at a time, all others remaining constant
options.C: Changing only the discount rate, in steps of 1%
options.D: Changing the accounting policies followed by the enterprise

e: Scenario analysis changes a consistent set of several variables together, as in an optimistic or pessimistic scenario, and sees the combined effect on the result. Sensitivity analysis, by contrast, changes one variable at a time with the others held constant.

q: Funds available are Rs 10,00,000. Three indivisible projects are available: A (outlay Rs 6,00,000, NPV Rs 1,80,000), B (outlay Rs 5,00,000, NPV Rs 1,50,000) and C (outlay Rs 4,00,000, NPV Rs 1,32,000). The combination that makes the best use of the funds is:

options.A: B and C together, with a total NPV of Rs 2,82,000
options.B: A alone, with an NPV of Rs 1,80,000
options.C: A and C together, with a total NPV of Rs 3,12,000
options.D: B alone, with an NPV of Rs 1,50,000

e: A plus C costs Rs 6,00,000 + Rs 4,00,000 = Rs 10,00,000, exactly the funds available, and gives NPV Rs 1,80,000 + Rs 1,32,000 = Rs 3,12,000. This beats B plus C at Rs 2,82,000 and either project alone, so it is the best feasible combination.

q: A project in operation can be abandoned now for a net realisation of Rs 6,25,000. The present value of the cash flows expected if it is continued is Rs 5,40,000. On financial grounds, the correct decision and its advantage are:

options.A: Continue the project, because its cash flows are positive
options.B: Abandon the project, gaining Rs 85,000 over continuing it
options.C: Abandon the project, gaining Rs 5,40,000
options.D: Continue the project, gaining Rs 85,000 over abandoning it

e: Abandonment realises Rs 6,25,000 against a continuation value of only Rs 5,40,000. Abandoning is better by Rs 6,25,000 - Rs 5,40,000 = Rs 85,000, so the project should be abandoned on financial grounds.

q: In the five-factor DuPont decomposition, the Return on Equity is broken down into the product of tax burden, interest burden, operating (EBIT) margin, total assets turnover and:

options.A: Dividend payout ratio
options.B: Current ratio
options.C: Financial leverage (assets to equity multiplier)
options.D: Inventory turnover ratio

e: The five-factor DuPont model splits Return on Equity into tax burden, interest burden, EBIT margin, total assets turnover and financial leverage, the assets-to-equity multiplier. Leverage is the fifth factor linking return on assets to return on equity.

q: Which of the following is NOT a component of the ordinary working expenses used in working out the Operating Ratio of a railway?

options.A: Wages and allowances of staff
options.B: Cost of fuel consumed in operations
options.C: Stores consumed for repairs and maintenance
options.D: Dividend payable to the General Revenues

e: The Operating Ratio uses ordinary working expenses such as wages, fuel and stores for repairs and maintenance. Dividend payable to General Revenues is an appropriation or financing charge, not a working expense of operations, so it is excluded.

q: The sales of an enterprise were Rs 4,00,000 in the base year (trend percentage = 100). Its sales in a later year are Rs 5,60,000. The trend percentage of sales in the later year is:
e: Trend percentage = Rs 5,60,000 / Rs 4,00,000 x 100 = 140. Trend analysis expresses each later year's figure as a percentage of the base year figure, which is taken as 100.

q: In a common-size balance sheet of an enterprise (total assets = Rs 20,00,000 taken as 100), stock amounts to Rs 3,00,000. Stock is expressed in the common-size statement as:
e: In a common-size balance sheet each item is shown as a percentage of total assets. Stock = Rs 3,00,000 / Rs 20,00,000 x 100 = 15 percent.

q: The net profit of an enterprise increased from Rs 2,50,000 in one year to Rs 3,00,000 in the next year. In a comparative statement, the change in net profit is shown as an increase of:
e: Percentage increase = (Rs 3,00,000 - Rs 2,50,000) / Rs 2,50,000 x 100 = Rs 50,000 / Rs 2,50,000 x 100 = 20 percent. In a comparative statement the change is measured on the earlier year's figure as the base.

q: An enterprise has a profit after tax of Rs 3,60,000, depreciation of Rs 90,000 and interest on term loans of Rs 1,50,000. Its debt service for the year (interest plus principal repayment of Rs 2,50,000) is Rs 4,00,000. Its Debt Service Coverage Ratio is:
e: Debt Service Coverage Ratio = (Rs 3,60,000 + Rs 90,000 + Rs 1,50,000) / Rs 4,00,000 = Rs 6,00,000 / Rs 4,00,000 = 1.50. Depreciation is added back as a non-cash charge and interest is added because it forms part of the debt service being covered.

q: The earnings of an enterprise before interest, tax and lease rentals are Rs 10,50,000. Its fixed charges consist of interest of Rs 2,00,000 and lease rentals of Rs 1,50,000. Its fixed charge coverage ratio is:

options.A: 3.0 times
options.B: 4.5 times
options.C: 9.0 times
options.D: 2.0 times

e: Fixed charge coverage = earnings before interest, tax and lease rentals / fixed charges = Rs 10,50,000 / (Rs 2,00,000 + Rs 1,50,000) = Rs 10,50,000 / Rs 3,50,000 = 3.0 times. Lease rentals are included because they are a fixed charge like interest.

q: An enterprise has cash in hand of Rs 80,000 and bank balances of Rs 70,000, and its current liabilities are Rs 3,75,000. Its cash ratio is:
e: Cash ratio = (cash in hand + bank balances) / current liabilities = (Rs 80,000 + Rs 70,000) / Rs 3,75,000 = Rs 1,50,000 / Rs 3,75,000 = 0.40. It is the strictest liquidity ratio, counting only cash and its nearest equivalents.

q: An enterprise has current assets of Rs 15,00,000, current liabilities of Rs 5,00,000 and stock of Rs 4,00,000. Its stock to working capital ratio is:
e: Working capital = Rs 15,00,000 - Rs 5,00,000 = Rs 10,00,000. Stock to working capital = Rs 4,00,000 / Rs 10,00,000 x 100 = 40 percent, showing the share of net working capital locked up in stock.

q: The sales of an enterprise are Rs 64,00,000 and its capital employed is Rs 16,00,000. Its sales to capital employed ratio is:

options.A: 0.25 times
options.B: 2.5 times
options.C: 3.0 times
options.D: 4.0 times

e: Sales to capital employed = Rs 64,00,000 / Rs 16,00,000 = 4.0 times. This turnover ratio shows how many rupees of sales are generated by each rupee of capital employed.

q: The profit before interest and tax of an enterprise is Rs 8,64,000 and its total assets (total resources) are Rs 48,00,000. Its return on total resources is:
e: Return on total resources = profit before interest and tax / total assets x 100 = Rs 8,64,000 / Rs 48,00,000 x 100 = 18 percent. Profit before interest and tax is used because total resources are financed by both owners and lenders.

q: The total sales of an enterprise are Rs 50,00,000, of which cash sales are Rs 10,00,000. Its average trade debtors are Rs 5,00,000. Its debtors turnover ratio is:

options.A: 10 times
options.B: 12.5 times
options.C: 5 times
options.D: 8 times

e: Credit sales = Rs 50,00,000 - Rs 10,00,000 = Rs 40,00,000. Debtors turnover = credit sales / average debtors = Rs 40,00,000 / Rs 5,00,000 = 8 times; cash sales are excluded because they create no debtors.

q: The profit before interest and tax of an enterprise is Rs 7,50,000 and the fixed interest charges payable are Rs 1,50,000. Expressed as fixed interest charges as a percentage of the profit before interest and tax, the income gearing is:
e: Income gearing here = fixed interest charges / profit before interest and tax x 100 = Rs 1,50,000 / Rs 7,50,000 x 100 = 20 percent. It shows the proportion of operating profit absorbed by fixed interest.

q: In computing the proprietors' funds of an enterprise for ratio analysis, which of the following is deducted (treated as a fictitious asset) rather than included?

options.A: Equity share capital
options.B: Preference share capital
options.C: General reserve
options.D: Preliminary expenses not written off

e: Preliminary expenses not written off are a fictitious asset with no realisable value. They are therefore deducted from, rather than included in, proprietors' funds for ratio analysis, unlike share capital and genuine reserves.

q: An enterprise revalues its fixed assets substantially upwards, creating a revaluation reserve, while its sales remain unchanged. Other things being equal, the immediate effect on its fixed assets turnover ratio will be that the ratio:

options.A: Falls, because the denominator (net fixed assets) has increased without any increase in sales
options.B: Rises, because the assets are now worth more
options.C: Remains unchanged, because revaluation is only a book entry
options.D: Cannot be determined without the current ratio

e: Fixed assets turnover = sales / net fixed assets. An upward revaluation raises the denominator while sales stay unchanged, so the ratio falls. The fall reflects the larger asset base in the books, not any decline in actual sales activity.

q: An enterprise transfers Rs 2,00,000 out of the year's profits to its general reserve. The effect of this transfer on the total proprietors' funds, and hence on ratios based on total proprietors' funds, is:

options.A: Total proprietors' funds increase by Rs 2,00,000
options.B: Total proprietors' funds decrease by Rs 2,00,000
options.C: Total proprietors' funds remain unchanged, the transfer being only an appropriation within the funds
options.D: Total proprietors' funds become nil to the extent of the transfer

e: Transferring profit to general reserve is only an appropriation within proprietors' funds: the profit and loss balance falls and the reserve rises by the same Rs 2,00,000. Total proprietors' funds therefore remain unchanged, and ratios based on that total are unaffected.

q: An enterprise judges its own ratios against the average ratios of its industry and finds them close to the average. The sound conclusion from this benchmarking is limited because:

options.A: Industry averages can never be computed correctly
options.B: The industry average is not necessarily the desirable or optimum level of performance
options.C: Ratios of different industries alone are comparable
options.D: An average conceals the figures of the best enterprise in the industry only

e: Being close to the industry average only shows the enterprise is typical, not that it is performing well. The industry average is not necessarily the desirable or optimum level, so benchmarking against it alone gives a limited conclusion.

q: Which of the following is an example of 'creative accounting' that can make an enterprise's reported ratios look better without any real improvement in performance?

options.A: Disclosing all contingent liabilities in the notes to accounts
options.B: Writing off a genuinely obsolete stock item promptly
options.C: Providing depreciation at the prescribed rates every year
options.D: Capitalising ordinary revenue expenses so that the year's profit and assets are both overstated

e: Capitalising ordinary revenue expenses defers them to the balance sheet instead of charging them to the year. This overstates both current profit and assets, flattering reported ratios without any real improvement in performance, which is creative accounting.

q: While comparing the sales and profits of an enterprise over a period of several years of rising prices, ratio and trend analysis can mislead because:

options.A: The comparison is in money terms, so a part of the apparent growth may merely reflect price increases rather than real growth in volume or efficiency
options.B: Sales figures of different years are never available on a comparable basis
options.C: Profits of earlier years are always overstated in the accounts
options.D: Rising prices always reduce the sales of every enterprise

e: In times of rising prices, sales and profit comparisons over years are in money terms. Part of the apparent growth may merely reflect higher prices rather than real growth in volume or efficiency, so trend and ratio analysis can mislead unless price changes are kept in mind.

q: 'Trading on equity' (financial leverage) works to the advantage of equity shareholders only when:

options.A: The enterprise has no preference share capital
options.B: The rate of interest on borrowed funds equals the dividend rate on equity shares
options.C: The dividend declared exceeds the profit earned in the year
options.D: The return earned on the capital employed exceeds the rate of interest payable on the borrowed funds

e: Trading on equity benefits equity shareholders only when the return earned on capital employed exceeds the rate of interest paid on borrowed funds. The surplus earned on borrowed capital then accrues to equity; if the return is lower, leverage works in reverse.

q: The profit available for equity shareholders of a company is Rs 9,00,000 and the equity dividend declared is Rs 3,00,000. Its dividend cover is:

options.A: 3.0 times
options.B: 0.33 times
options.D: 1.5 times

e: Dividend cover = profit available for equity shareholders / equity dividend = Rs 9,00,000 / Rs 3,00,000 = 3.0 times. It shows how many times the declared dividend is covered by available earnings.

q: A company's share is quoted in the market at Rs 180 and its book value per share is Rs 120. Its market price to book value ratio is:
e: Market price to book value = Rs 180 / Rs 120 = 1.5. The share trades at one and a half times its book value per share, indicating the market values it above the net assets recorded per share.

q: The total outside liabilities of an enterprise are Rs 10,50,000 and its proprietors' funds are Rs 17,50,000. The ratio of total outside liabilities to proprietors' funds is:
e: Ratio of total outside liabilities to proprietors' funds = Rs 10,50,000 / Rs 17,50,000 = 0.60. It compares what the enterprise owes to outsiders with the owners' stake in the business.

q: The budget committee of a large enterprise is normally constituted as:

options.A: A committee of the statutory auditors and the internal auditors of the enterprise
options.B: The chief executive as chairman, with the heads of the main functional departments such as production, sales, finance and personnel as members
options.C: A committee consisting only of the shareholders of the enterprise
options.D: The budget officer sitting alone, without any functional manager

e: A budget committee is normally headed by the chief executive and includes the heads of the main functional departments such as production, sales, finance and personnel. This composition lets the functional budgets be coordinated and conflicts resolved at one forum.

q: The output of an enterprise fluctuates widely from month to month because its demand is highly seasonal, so that in some months the plant works at full capacity and in others at barely half of it. For controlling its costs fairly, the enterprise should prepare:

options.A: A flexible budget, which can be recast for the actual level of activity attained in each month
options.B: A fixed budget for the peak level of activity, to be applied unchanged in every month
options.C: No budget at all, since the output is not steady
options.D: Only a cash budget, since cost control is not possible in such an enterprise

e: A flexible budget is recast for the actual level of activity attained, so costs can be compared with what they should have been at that output. With widely fluctuating seasonal output, a fixed budget would compare costs at unlike activity levels and control unfairly.

q: In budgetary control, an adverse variance has been reported and its cause has been ascertained. The step that makes the system a system of control, and not merely a system of reporting, is:

options.A: Filing the variance report without any further action until the year ends
options.B: Punishing the manager of the department concerned, whatever the cause of the variance
options.C: Taking remedial or corrective action by the manager responsible so that performance is brought back in line with the budget, the budget itself being revised only where the assumptions underlying it have changed
options.D: Revising the budget figures retrospectively so that no variance remains

e: Budgetary control is complete only when an adverse variance leads to remedial action by the responsible manager to bring performance back in line with the budget. Mere reporting is not control, and the budget is revised only where its underlying assumptions have changed.

q: The output of a manufacturer is restricted neither by plant capacity nor by the demand for its product, but by the limited quantity of an imported raw material that is in short supply. In preparing the budgets of this enterprise, the principal budget factor is:

options.A: The cash balance available with the enterprise
options.B: The number of workers employed in the factory
options.C: The selling price of the finished product
options.D: The availability of that raw material, and all the functional budgets must be built within the quantity of the material that can be obtained

e: The principal budget factor is the factor that limits output and around which all budgets must be built. Here it is the availability of the scarce imported raw material, since neither capacity nor demand is the binding constraint.

q: A factory has to deliver 48,000 finished units during the budget period. It expects to have 4,000 units in work-in-progress at the beginning of the period and 6,000 units in work-in-progress at the end of the period. The number of units to be put into production during the period is:

options.A: 48,000 units
options.B: 50,000 units
options.C: 46,000 units
options.D: 54,000 units

e: Units to be put into production = units to be delivered + closing work-in-progress - opening work-in-progress = 48,000 + 6,000 - 4,000 = 50,000 units. The extra 2,000 units build up the closing work-in-progress stock.
